claim: Human cells lacking RIF1 are highly sensitive to replication inhibitors.
source: Human cells lacking RIF1 are highly sensitive to replication inhibitors, but the reasons for this sensitivity have been enigmatic.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact and is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: RIF1 must be present both during replication stress and in the ensuing recovery period to promote cell survival.
source: Here, we show that RIF1 must be present both during replication stress and in the ensuing recovery period to promote cell survival.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by the staged depletion experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: RIF1-Long alone can protect cells against replication inhibition.
source: Of two isoforms produced by alternative splicing, we find that RIF1-Long alone can protect cells against replication inhibition, but RIF1-Short is incapable of mediating protection.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by colony formation assays comparing RIF1-L and RIF1-S shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: RIF1-Short is incapable of mediating protection against replication inhibition.
source: Of two isoforms produced by alternative splicing, we find that RIF1-Long alone can protect cells against replication inhibition, but RIF1-Short is incapable of mediating protection.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by colony formation assays shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: RIF1-Long is required to promote the formation of 53BP1 nuclear bodies that protect unrepaired damage sites in G1 phase following replication stress.
source: Consistent with this isoform-specific role, RIF1-Long is required to promote the formation of the 53BP1 nuclear bodies that protect unrepaired damage sites in the G1 phase following replication stress.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5.

claim: During double-strand break repair, RIF1 is recruited by 53BP1, dependent upon phosphorylation of 53BP1 by ATM.
source: During double-strand break repair, RIF1 is recruited by 53BP1, dependent upon phosphorylation of 53BP1 by ATM (Chapman et al., 2013; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Di Virgilio et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RIF1 and 53BP1 recruit Shieldin and suppress BRCA1 recruitment to damage sites.
source: Together RIF1 and 53BP1 recruit Shieldin and suppress BRCA1 recruitment to damage sites, opposing homologous recombination-based repair and favouring non-homologous end joining (Bunting et al., 2010; Setiaputra and Durocher, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RIF1 and 53BP1 oppose homologous recombination-based repair and favour non-homologous end joining.
source: Together RIF1 and 53BP1 recruit Shieldin and suppress BRCA1 recruitment to damage sites, opposing homologous recombination-based repair and favouring non-homologous end joining (Bunting et al., 2010; Setiaputra and Durocher, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Aphidicolin interrupts replication fork progression by inhibiting the replicative DNA polymerases α, δ and ε.
source: Replication stress can be induced by various conditions including drugs such as Aphidicolin, which interrupts replication fork progression by inhibiting the replicative DNA polymerases α, δ and ε (Syvaoja et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Replication stress leads to genomic instability, mutation and eventually disease.
source: Replication stress leads to genomic instability, mutation and eventually disease (Burrell et al., 2013; Kerzendorfer et al., 2013; Ogi et al., 2012), so understanding the cellular response is central for understanding accurate genome duplication and the action of replication inhibitors as anti-cancer drugs (Feng et al., 2003; Imai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RIF1-deficient cells are acutely sensitive to replication stress.
source: RIF1-deficient cells are acutely sensitive to replication stress, in fact appearing to be more sensitive to replication inhibitors than to double-strand break-inducing agents (Buonomo et al., 2009), suggesting that protection from stress is a critical RIF1 function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: RIF1-deficient cells appear to be more sensitive to replication inhibitors than to double-strand break-inducing agents.
source: RIF1-deficient cells are acutely sensitive to replication stress, in fact appearing to be more sensitive to replication inhibitors than to double-strand break-inducing agents (Buonomo et al., 2009), suggesting that protection from stress is a critical RIF1 function.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: RIF1 acts as a Protein Phosphatase 1 (PP1) 'substrate-targeting subunit' that suppresses replication origin initiation by directing PP1 to dephosphorylate the MCM replicative helicase complex.
source: RIF1 acts as a Protein Phosphatase 1 (PP1) 'substrate-targeting subunit' (Peti et al., 2013) that suppresses replication origin initiation by directing PP1 to dephosphorylate the MCM replicative helicase complex (Alver et al., 2017; Davé et al., 2014; Gnan et al., 2020; Hiraga et al., 2017; Hiraga et al., 2014; Mattarocci et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RIF1 stimulates origin licensing during G1 phase.
source: RIF1 moreover stimulates origin licensing during G1 phase, and protects replication forks from unscheduled degradation (Garzón et al., 2019; Hiraga et al., 2017; Mukherjee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RIF1 protects replication forks from unscheduled degradation.
source: RIF1 moreover stimulates origin licensing during G1 phase, and protects replication forks from unscheduled degradation (Garzón et al., 2019; Hiraga et al., 2017; Mukherjee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and by experimental data in Figure 3F.

claim: During anaphase, RIF1 is recruited to ultra-fine anaphase bridges (UFBs), along with the BLM and PICH proteins that ensure proper chromosome segregation.
source: During anaphase, RIF1 is recruited to ultra-fine anaphase bridges (UFBs), along with the BLM and PICH proteins that ensure proper chromosome segregation (Hengeveld et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and by imaging data in Figure 1H and Figure 4.

claim: UFBs are believed to correspond to unresolved topological entanglements that escape checkpoint surveillance and persist into mitosis.
source: UFBs are believed to correspond to unresolved topological entanglements that escape checkpoint surveillance and persist into mitosis (Bergoglio et al., 2013; Bhowmick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Unresolved DNA damage that passes to daughter cells leads to the formation of 53BP1 nuclear bodies during G1 phase, which protect the damaged DNA.
source: Unresolved DNA damage that passes to daughter cells leads to the formation of 53BP1 nuclear bodies during G1 phase, which protect the damaged DNA (Bruhn et al., 2014; Lukas et al., 2011; Moreno et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RIF1 has been described as functioning at the midbody during cytokinesis.
source: RIF1 has also recently been described as functioning at the midbody during cytokinesis (Bhowmick et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The human RIF1 transcript undergoes alternative splicing producing two protein isoforms: a long variant of 2472 amino acids ('RIF1-L'), and a short variant ('RIF1-S') which lacks 26 amino acids close to the C-terminus of the protein.
source: The human RIF1 transcript undergoes alternative splicing producing two protein isoforms: a long variant of 2472 amino acids ('RIF1-L'), and a short variant ('RIF1-S') which lacks 26 amino acids close to the C-terminus of the protein (Xu and Blackburn, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: RIF1-S was reported to be more abundant in various cancer cell lines.
source: RIF1-S was reported to be more abundant in various cancer cell lines (Xu and Blackburn, 2004), hinting at distinct effects of the isoforms.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Studies using cloned RIF1 have predominantly used RIF1-S without testing for distinct functions of the isoforms.
source: Although RIF1-L was designated the canonical form, studies using cloned RIF1 have predominantly used RIF1-S (Batenburg et al., 2017; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2010; Xu and Blackburn, 2004), without testing for distinct functions of the isoforms.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HEK293 cells depleted for RIF1 are sensitive to Aphidicolin.
source: First, we confirmed in a colony formation assay (CFA) that HEK293 cells depleted for RIF1 are sensitive to the DNA polymerase inhibitor Aphidicolin (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: HCT116 cells deleted for both copies of RIF1 are sensitive to Aphidicolin.
source: HCT116 cells deleted for both copies of RIF1 were also sensitive (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Treatment for 24 hr with DOX and Auxin led to near-complete degradation of RIF1 in the mAC-RIF1 cell line.
source: Treatment for 24 hr with DOX and Auxin led to near-complete degradation of RIF1, as visualised by western blotting (Figure 1E) and microscopy (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claim: Degradation of mAC-RIF1 was largely complete after 3 hr of Auxin treatment.
source: Degradation was largely complete after 3 hr of Auxin treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), whilst expression was restored to almost normal levels 5 hr after Auxin removal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of mAC-RIF1 was restored to almost normal levels 5 hr after Auxin removal.
source: Degradation was largely complete after 3 hr of Auxin treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), whilst expression was restored to almost normal levels 5 hr after Auxin removal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In live-cell imaging experiments, a pattern of numerous mAC-RIF1 foci was observed throughout S phase nuclei.
source: In live-cell imaging experiments we observed a pattern of numerous mAC-RIF1 foci throughout S phase nuclei (Figure 1G, top row), often with 3–6 prominent foci superimposed on a pattern of more numerous smaller foci, consistent with previous immunofluorescence studies (Buonomo et al., 2009; Xu and Blackburn, 2004; Yamazaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1G and citations to previous literature.

claim: In prometaphase, mAC-RIF1 exhibits a circumpolar localisation pattern similar to that described for kinetochores.
source: In prometaphase mAC-RIF1 exhibits a novel, circumpolar localisation pattern similar to that described for kinetochores (Figure 1G, second row, showing polar view of condensed chromosomes) (Magidson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1G and a citation to previous literature.

claim: At anaphase, mAC-RIF1 was sometimes observed at bridge structures where it colocalised with the bridge marker protein BLM.
source: At anaphase, even in unperturbed cells, mAC-RIF1 was sometimes observed at bridge structures (Figure 1G, third row) where it colocalised with the bridge marker protein BLM, but not always with conventional DNA dyes (Figure 1H, bottom panel) (Barefield and Karlseder, 2012; Chan et al., 2007; Hengeveld et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1G and 1H, and citations to previous literature.

claim: At telophase, mAC-RIF1 formed multiple small foci associated with separated chromosomes.
source: At telophase, mAC-RIF1 formed multiple small foci associated with separated chromosomes (Figure 1G, bottom row), as described previously (Xu and Blackburn, 2004; Yamazaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1G and citations to previous literature.

claim: Intense RIF1 foci accumulated through S phase and G2, but disappeared by metaphase.
source: Time-lapse imaging of HCT116 mAC-RIF1 cells containing an mCherry-tagged PCNA revealed intense RIF1 foci that accumulated through S phase and G2 (Video 1), but disappeared by metaphase (Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Video 1 and Video 2.

claim: RIF1 signal was absent for a short period at metaphase, quickly followed by reappearance of numerous smaller foci on telophase chromosomes.
source: RIF1 signal was absent for a short period at metaphase, quickly followed by reappearance of numerous smaller foci on telophase chromosomes.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Video 2.

claim: Prolonged auxin-induced degradation of RIF1 caused sensitivity to Aphidicolin, comparable to an HCT116 RIF1-knockout cell line.
source: Prolonged auxin-induced degradation of RIF1 caused sensitivity to Aphidicolin, comparable to an HCT116 RIF1-knockout cell line (RIF1 KO) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, Figure 3B lane 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, and Figure 3B.

claim: Cells depleted of RIF1 only during the replication stress treatment period showed sensitivity similar to cells depleted of RIF1 throughout the entire experiment.
source: Cells depleted of RIF1 only during the replication stress treatment period (condition I) showed sensitivity similar to the RIF1-depleted (RIF1-) condition, displaying a mean surviving fraction of 33% (data from two biological replicates shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Cells depleted of RIF1 only during the recovery period showed high sensitivity similar to cells depleted of RIF1 throughout the entire experiment.
source: Cells depleted of RIF1 only during the recovery period (condition II) also showed high sensitivity, again similar to RIF1- with a mean surviving fraction of 26% (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Molecular functions of RIF1 occurring both during and after a stressed S phase are important for survival.
source: These results indicate that molecular functions of RIF1 occurring both during and after a stressed S phase are important for survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the staged depletion experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Transcripts encoding both RIF1-L and RIF1-S isoforms are widely expressed in various tissues in vivo.
source: We confirmed that transcripts encoding both the isoforms are widely expressed in various tissues in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and are present in U2OS and HEK293 cell lines (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mAC-RIF1-L cell line showed resistance to Aphidicolin very similar to that of the parent mAC-RIF1 cells.
source: We found that whilst the mAC-RIF1-L cell line showed resistance to Aphidicolin very similar to that of the parent mAC-RIF1 cells (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, black and red lines), the mAC-RIF1-S isoform in contrast conferred little protection against drug, producing sensitivity similar to that of cells lacking RIF1 altogether (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, grey and dotted lines).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The mAC-RIF1-S isoform conferred little protection against Aphidicolin, producing sensitivity similar to that of cells lacking RIF1 altogether.
source: We found that whilst the mAC-RIF1-L cell line showed resistance to Aphidicolin very similar to that of the parent mAC-RIF1 cells (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, black and red lines), the mAC-RIF1-S isoform in contrast conferred little protection against drug, producing sensitivity similar to that of cells lacking RIF1 altogether (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, grey and dotted lines).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In HEK293-derived cell lines, RIF1-L was able to protect against Aphidicolin treatment, whilst RIF1-S could not.
source: We found that also in this cell line RIF1-L was able to protect against Aphidicolin treatment, whilst RIF1-S could not (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D and E, red and grey lines).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3D and E.

claim: In HEK293-derived cell lines, RIF1-L was able to protect cells from Hydroxyurea treatment whilst RIF1-S could not.
source: Similarly, in the same cell line RIF1-L was able to protect cells from Hydroxyurea treatment whilst RIF1-S could not (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3F.

claim: Both RIF1-L and RIF1-S isoforms are equally effective in preventing hyperphosphorylation of the MCM complex.
source: We found that both isoforms however appear equally functional in the previously described mechanisms through which RIF1 affects DNA replication. The isoforms are equally effective in preventing hyperphosphorylation of the MCM complex (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A) and protecting nascent DNA at blocked replication forks (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Both RIF1-L and RIF1-S isoforms are equally effective in protecting nascent DNA at blocked replication forks.
source: We found that both isoforms however appear equally functional in the previously described mechanisms through which RIF1 affects DNA replication. The isoforms are equally effective in preventing hyperphosphorylation of the MCM complex (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A) and protecting nascent DNA at blocked replication forks (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: No significant differences were observed between cells expressing RIF1-S or RIF1-L in replication fork speed.
source: Nor did we observe significant differences between cells expressing RIF1-S or RIF1-L in replication fork speed (as assessed by nascent DNA tract length; Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), bulk DNA synthesis levels (as measured by flow cytometry; Figure 3—figure supplement 4C), or replisome density (based on PCNA loading on chromatin; Figure 3—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: No significant differences were observed between cells expressing RIF1-S or RIF1-L in bulk DNA synthesis levels.
source: Nor did we observe significant differences between cells expressing RIF1-S or RIF1-L in replication fork speed (as assessed by nascent DNA tract length; Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), bulk DNA synthesis levels (as measured by flow cytometry; Figure 3—figure supplement 4C), or replisome density (based on PCNA loading on chromatin; Figure 3—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4C.

claim: No significant differences were observed between cells expressing RIF1-S or RIF1-L in replisome density.
source: Nor did we observe significant differences between cells expressing RIF1-S or RIF1-L in replication fork speed (as assessed by nascent DNA tract length; Figure 3—figure supplement 4B), bulk DNA synthesis levels (as measured by flow cytometry; Figure 3—figure supplement 4C), or replisome density (based on PCNA loading on chromatin; Figure 3—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4D.

claim: RIF1-L-pp1bs protein was almost as effective as wild-type RIF1-L in conferring resistance to Aphidicolin.
source: This 'RIF1-L-pp1bs' protein was almost as effective as wild-type RIF1-L in conferring resistance to Aphidicolin (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 5A), indicating that RIF1-L acts largely independent of PP1 function in protecting cells from the effects of Aphidicolin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A.

claim: RIF1-L acts largely independent of PP1 function in protecting cells from the effects of Aphidicolin.
source: This 'RIF1-L-pp1bs' protein was almost as effective as wild-type RIF1-L in conferring resistance to Aphidicolin (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 5A), indicating that RIF1-L acts largely independent of PP1 function in protecting cells from the effects of Aphidicolin.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that PP1-binding mutant RIF1-L retains protective function.

claim: The function of RIF1 in protecting from replication stress is distinct from its previously known roles in replication control, which do require PP1.
source: This independence from PP1 reinforces the evidence that the function of RIF1 in protecting from replication stress is distinct from its previously known roles in replication control, which do require PP1.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of PP1-dependent and PP1-independent functions of RIF1.

claim: No clear difference was found in rates of UFB formation in the HCT116 RIF1-L or RIF1-S cells after ICRF-193 treatment.
source: We found no clear difference in rates of UFB formation in the HCT116 RIF1-L or RIF1-S cells after ICRF-193 treatment (Figure 4Aii, left), and both RIF1-L and RIF1-S were localised at the UFBs formed (Figure 4Ai, and Figure 4Aii, right).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4Ai and 4Aii.

claim: Both RIF1-L and RIF1-S were localised at UFBs formed after ICRF-193 treatment.
source: We found no clear difference in rates of UFB formation in the HCT116 RIF1-L or RIF1-S cells after ICRF-193 treatment (Figure 4Aii, left), and both RIF1-L and RIF1-S were localised at the UFBs formed (Figure 4Ai, and Figure 4Aii, right).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4Ai and 4Aii.

claim: Treatment of HCT116-based cell lines with Aphidicolin did not induce UFBs, but rather increased the incidence of anaphase chromosome bridges.
source: Treatment of these HCT116-based cell lines with Aphidicolin surprisingly did not induce UFBs, but rather increased the incidence of anaphase chromosome bridges (defined as bridge structures that stain with DAPI) (Figure 4Ai, Bi).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4Ai and 4Bi.

claim: Anaphase bridges after Aphidicolin treatment were formed at similar rates in the RIF1-L and RIF1-S-expressing cells.
source: These anaphase bridges were formed at similar rates in the RIF1-L and RIF1-S-expressing cells (Figure 4Bii, left) and both RIF1-L and RIF1-S were localised to these anaphase bridges (Figure 4Bi, Bii, right).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4Bi and 4Bii.

claim: Both RIF1-L and RIF1-S were localised to anaphase bridges formed after Aphidicolin treatment.
source: These anaphase bridges were formed at similar rates in the RIF1-L and RIF1-S-expressing cells (Figure 4Bii, left) and both RIF1-L and RIF1-S were localised to these anaphase bridges (Figure 4Bi, Bii, right).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4Bi and 4Bii.

claim: Both RIF1 isoforms can localise effectively to both anaphase bridge and UFB structures.
source: Overall therefore, both RIF1 isoforms can localise effectively to both anaphase bridge and UFB structures; and the loss of RIF1 does not greatly affect the rate at which such bridge structures occur.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The loss of RIF1 does not greatly affect the rate at which anaphase bridge or UFB structures occur.
source: Overall therefore, both RIF1 isoforms can localise effectively to both anaphase bridge and UFB structures; and the loss of RIF1 does not greatly affect the rate at which such bridge structures occur.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Neither chromatin breaks nor MiDAS were significantly elevated in cells lacking RIF1 after Aphidicolin treatment.
source: However, neither chromatin breaks nor MiDAS were significantly elevated in cells lacking RIF1 after Aphidicolin treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: The parental mAC-RIF1 cell line showed an elevated fraction of cells with multiple large 53BP1 NBs after Aphidicolin treatment.
source: The parental (mAC-RIF1) cell line showed an elevated fraction of cells with multiple large 53BP1 NBs (Figure 5A top row, 5B black bars and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C top left panel), as expected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, 5B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A reduced number of 53BP1 NBs were observed in RIF1-KO cells after Aphidicolin treatment.
source: In contrast, a reduced number of 53BP1 NBs were observed in RIF1-KO cells (Figure 5A bottom row, 5B open bars, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C bottom right panel), demonstrating that RIF1 contributes to the formation of 53BP1 bodies after replication stress.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, 5B, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RIF1 contributes to the formation of 53BP1 bodies after replication stress.
source: In contrast, a reduced number of 53BP1 NBs were observed in RIF1-KO cells (Figure 5A bottom row, 5B open bars, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C bottom right panel), demonstrating that RIF1 contributes to the formation of 53BP1 bodies after replication stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of 53BP1 NB formation in RIF1-expressing and RIF1-KO cells.

claim: mAC-RIF1-L localised normally with 53BP1 bodies, and supported their formation at a near normal rate.
source: Examining the cell lines expressing only Long or Short RIF1 isoforms, we found that mAC-RIF1-L localised normally with 53BP1 bodies, and supported their formation at a near normal rate (Figure 5A second row, 5B,C red bars and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C top right panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, 5B, 5C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The number of 53BP1 NBs formed in mAC-RIF1-S cells was similar to that in RIF1-KO cells.
source: In contrast, the number of 53BP1 NBs formed in mAC-RIF1-S cells was similar to that in RIF1-KO cells, and mAC-RIF1-S showed reduced co-localisation with the 53BP1 bodies (Figure 5A third row, 5B,C grey bars and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C bottom left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, 5B, 5C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: mAC-RIF1-S showed reduced co-localisation with 53BP1 bodies.
source: In contrast, the number of 53BP1 NBs formed in mAC-RIF1-S cells was similar to that in RIF1-KO cells, and mAC-RIF1-S showed reduced co-localisation with the 53BP1 bodies (Figure 5A third row, 5B,C grey bars and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C bottom left panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, 5B, 5C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The reduced rate of 53BP1 NB formation in mAC-RIF1-S cells was not due to reduced abundance of 53BP1 in mAC-RIF1-S when compared to mAC-RIF1-L cells.
source: The reduced rate of 53BP1 NB formation in mAC-RIF1-S cells was not due to reduced abundance of 53BP1 in mAC-RIF1-S when compared to mAC-RIF1-L cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The two RIF1 isoforms differ in their effectiveness in promoting 53BP1 nuclear body formation following replication stress, with RIF1-L but not RIF1-S functional in this role.
source: The two RIF1 isoforms therefore differ in their effectiveness in promoting 53BP1 nuclear body formation following replication stress, with RIF1-L but not RIF1-S functional in this role.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: 53BP1 nuclear bodies are known to protect DNA damaged as a consequence of Aphidicolin treatment.
source: Since 53BP1 nuclear bodies are known to protect DNA damaged as a consequence of Aphidicolin treatment (Lukas et al., 2011), the defect in 53BP1 body formation in the absence of RIF1-L is likely to be an important factor in the replication stress sensitivity of RIF1-deficient cells, and may explain the isoform specificity of the replication stress protection function of RIF1.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The defect in 53BP1 body formation in the absence of RIF1-L is likely to be an important factor in the replication stress sensitivity of RIF1-deficient cells.
source: Since 53BP1 nuclear bodies are known to protect DNA damaged as a consequence of Aphidicolin treatment (Lukas et al., 2011), the defect in 53BP1 body formation in the absence of RIF1-L is likely to be an important factor in the replication stress sensitivity of RIF1-deficient cells, and may explain the isoform specificity of the replication stress protection function of RIF1.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between 53BP1 NB formation defects and replication stress sensitivity.

claim: The defect in 53BP1 body formation may explain the isoform specificity of the replication stress protection function of RIF1.
source: Since 53BP1 nuclear bodies are known to protect DNA damaged as a consequence of Aphidicolin treatment (Lukas et al., 2011), the defect in 53BP1 body formation in the absence of RIF1-L is likely to be an important factor in the replication stress sensitivity of RIF1-deficient cells, and may explain the isoform specificity of the replication stress protection function of RIF1.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed correlation.

claim: RIF1 depletion in U2OS cells caused a reproducible reduction in the number of 53BP1 NBs after Aphidicolin treatment.
source: To test in a different cell line whether RIF1 contributes to the number of 53BP1 nuclear bodies formed, we examined U2OS cells depleted of RIF1, 12 hr after release from a 24 hr Aphidicolin treatment (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D). We found that RIF1 depletion caused a reproducible reduction in the number of NBs, similar to that observed in our HCT116-derived cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Depleting TopBP1 substantially reduced the rate of 53BP1 NB colocalisation with RIF1-L.
source: We found that depleting TopBP1 substantially reduced the rate of 53BP1 NB colocalisation with RIF1-L (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: TopBP1 is needed for effective localisation of RIF1-L with 53BP1 NBs.
source: We conclude that TopBP1 is needed for effective localisation of RIF1-L with 53BP1 NBs, potentially enabling the specific function of RIF1-L in recovery from Aphidicolin treatment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced RIF1-L/53BP1 NB colocalisation upon TopBP1 depletion.

claim: RIF1-S appears competent to fulfil the known functions of RIF1 in DNA replication management.
source: This deficiency of RIF1-S function was initially surprising, since RIF1-S appears competent to fulfil the known functions of RIF1 in DNA replication management—in particular RIF1-S is able to support replication licensing and control MCM phosphorylation (Hiraga et al., 2017 and Figure 3E), and to protect against nascent DNA degradation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3F, and a citation to previous literature.

claim: All known functions of RIF1 in replication control (promotion of replication licensing, control of MCM phosphorylation, and nascent DNA protection) depend on PP1 recruitment by RIF1.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and experimental data shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.
